newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Van Miert mulls grace period for beer, oil sales.
newsitem.headline: Van Miert mulls grace period for beer, oil sales.

text.p: Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert is considering extending until 1999 two block exemptions allowing exclusive supply agreements in the beer and oil industries, the Commission said in a statement on Wednesday.
"Van Miert is looking at the possibility of prolonging the duration of the validity of these two regulations until 31 December 1999," the statement said.

The announcement comes as a relief especially for British brewers who feared that the rules covering supply arrangements with pubs would be scrapped altogether when the EU decides on its future policy on exclusive distribution deals.
"We support the continuation of the block exemptions and expect they will be retained beyond that date," James Wilson, Public Policy Executive at Bass Plc's Brussels office, said.

The regulations at stake, 1983/83/EEC and 1984/83/EEC, cover agreements by which a supplier appoints a reseller as his exclusive distributor in a given area, on the one hand, and arrangements by which a reseller agrees to buy all his products from one supplier only, on the other hand.
In practice this means beer-supply deals particularly between British breweries and pubs owned by them -- usually described as tied houses -- are exempted from competition rules.

It also allows oil companies to conclude exclusive supply accords with petrol stations for motor fuels. Lubricants and items sold in convenience shops are not covered although the oil industry would like this to be the case.
The two texts adopted in 1993 cover tens of thousands of agreements.

They were due for review at the end of 1997, but the industries concerned were worried that an upcoming green paper on vertical restraints -- the term for exclusive supply and distributions arrangements -- would mean their death sentence.
The Commission's statement did not say when Van Miert would propose extending the rules. The final decision must be taken by the full Commission.
But the much-awaited green paper was expected to be adopted at the beginning of 1997, the statement said. This is more than a year than initially announced.
The Commission will then engage in consultations with all interested parties before deciding on future policy.
British brewers have already made it known they would like their so-called beer block exemption to be extended by a minimum period of 15 years.
